name: Conversation, Not Just Announcements
title: Conversation, Not Just Announcements
answer: Two way translated messaging turns school announcements into real conversations, because parents can reply in their own language and get replies in theirs. It matters because families can ask questions and share what they know about their children, rather than only receiving information. The book treats this as everyday communication, not a channel for sensitive matters.

sections.body: This idea is that family communication should flow in both directions, not only from school to home. Translated two way messaging lets parents write to teachers in their own language and receive answers in that same language, so an announcement becomes a conversation. The problem it solves is one way communication that leaves families unable to respond, ask questions, or share concerns and knowledge about their children. When parents can reply, teachers learn things about their students that a broadcast message would never surface. The book frames this as the basic standard for good family communication.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, teachers use two way translated messaging so parents can reply to messages in their own language and read the teacher's replies in theirs. Teachers are expected to answer family messages promptly and personally, and any AI drafted reply should still sound like the teacher and respond to what the parent actually said. The book gives no grade band variations for this practice. It does say that if a conversation turns to something sensitive, the teacher should move it to a call with an interpreter. The translation tool is meant for everyday conversation, not for serious matters.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels the evidence here as research from health care, not from schools. It states that research in health care has documented translation errors in real conversations, not just documents, citing Strechen et al., 2025. That finding is used to show that two way messaging carries the same accuracy risks as any translation. The book does not present school based studies or figures for this idea. The evidence it offers is a warning about translation accuracy drawn from another field.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The book sets clear limits. A reply that feels automated can do more harm than no reply at all, because families notice when they are being handled rather than heard, so the teacher must stay personally present in the exchange. Translation carries accuracy risks in live conversation just as it does in documents, so sensitive topics should leave the messaging channel and become a call with an interpreter. The translation tool is for everyday conversation only. The decisions about when to move a conversation to a call, and what a reply should say, stay with the teacher.
